title: Judges 1:22–26
context: The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel, and the LORD is with them. They send to spy out the city, whose former name was Luz. The watchers see a man coming out, and they promise to deal kindly with him if he will show them the entrance. He does so. They strike the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go. He goes into the land of the Hittites, builds a city, and calls its name Luz, which is its name to this day. Both traditions read the unit as a success under the LORD’s presence, obtained through a spared informant and a kept word of kindness. Some readers have compared the sparing of this man and his family with Rahab’s household at Jericho; that is a possible parallel, not a claimed typology or a consensus, and it is not a contrast between the two traditions. The later site of this second Luz is not named, and it should not be fixed as if the verse had settled it.

verses.text: The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, “and the LORD was with them.” The northern campaign opens under the same kind of notice already given to Judah.

Arminian readers hear the Joseph tribes actually going up, and they hear the LORD’s presence as the true ground of what follows. Presence does not cancel the need to go; it attends the going.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that “the LORD was with them” is the narrator’s first word about this assault, as it was with Judah in the hill country. Bethel will fall under that presence, not under Joseph’s cunning alone.

Both traditions take the verse as a campaign begun with God’s help, shared ground at the turn from Judah and Benjamin to Joseph.

verses.text: The house of Joseph sent to spy out Bethel. (The name of the city before that was Luz.)
verses.arminianNotes:
The house of Joseph sent to spy out Bethel. The name of the city before that was Luz. The taking is prepared by a reconnaissance, and the older name is recorded.

Arminian readers hear a careful, human means. They must actually spy out the city; the LORD’s being with them in verse 22 does not make inquiry unnecessary.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the spying and the former-name notice as the narrator’s preparation for the entrance they will be shown. Luz is identified so that the later renaming in verse 26 will be clear.

Both traditions read the verse as the scouting of Bethel, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: The watchers saw a man come out of the city, and they said to him, “Please show us the entrance into the city, and we will deal kindly with you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The watchers saw a man come out of the city, and they said to him, “Please show us the entrance into the city, and we will deal kindly with you.” Kindness is pledged in exchange for the way in.

Arminian readers hear a real offer that will have to be kept. The man is asked to show the entrance, and the house of Joseph binds itself to deal kindly with him if he does.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same pledge of kindness. The watchers do not storm a way of their own devising first; they seek an entrance and vow to treat the man well.

Both traditions take the words as a true commitment, the basis of the sparing in the next verse, without forcing a comparison with other kindness scenes as if it were required.

verses.text: He showed them the entrance into the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword; but they let the man and all his family go.
verses.arminianNotes:
He showed them the entrance into the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword; but they let the man and all his family go. The city falls; the promised kindness is kept.

Arminian readers hear both the stroke and the mercy. The man does what he was asked, and his whole family is allowed to go; the house of Joseph honors its word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the entrance is shown, the city is struck, and the family is let go. The pledge of verse 24 is not broken in the taking.

Some readers compare this sparing with Rahab’s house; that parallel is available, not required, and it is not a point of contrast between the two traditions. Both take the verse as judgment on the city and kept kindness to the man.

verses.text: The man went into the land of the Hittites, built a city, and called its name Luz, which is its name to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man went into the land of the Hittites, built a city, and called its name Luz, which is its name “to this day.” The spared man founds another Luz under the old name.

Arminian readers hear a life and a city given back on the far side of the escape. The narrator still knows that place in his own day; the exact site in the land of the Hittites is not fixed by this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the building and the naming as the outcome of the kindness already shown. “to this day” is the narrator’s stamp, as in verse 21; it is not, by itself, a date.

Both traditions read the second Luz as a real settlement named by the spared man, without inventing a consensus about its later location.
